{"id": "69:10/q04", "question": "What does calling Him “their Lord” convey?", "turns_on": "The notes point to either the Lord's benefaction or the contrast with Pharaoh's claimed lordship.", "positions": [{"id": "69:10/q04/p1", "position": "It makes disobedience culpable because He created, provided for, and guided them.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says He gave them faculties and provision and sent guidance, while they wrongly supposed their benefactor could not harm them."}, {"id": "69:10/q04/p2", "position": "It exposes their error in treating Pharaoh as their lord.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the possessive hints at their worship of Pharaoh and their treating him as a god."}]}
{"id": "69:10/q05", "question": "How does the disobedience clause relate to the preceding account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:10/q05/p1", "position": "It elaborates the preceding statement of their sin.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the elaboration of Noah's people's sin in 54:9. Al-Ālūsī says disobedience explains their coming with the sinful deed just mentioned."}]}
{"id": "69:10/q06", "question": "Who seized them?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:10/q06/p1", "position": "God seized the disobedient communities.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī says God seized each community with punishment."}]}
{"id": "69:10/q07", "question": "What does the taking mean, and what happened to the peoples?", "turns_on": "The notes variously explain the event as destruction of the peoples or stress the seizure's final, unbearable character.", "positions": [{"id": "69:10/q07/p1", "position": "God destroyed them completely with punishments suited to each people.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says 'taking' means destruction, comparing 6:44, and says Pharaoh's taking was drowning, comparing 54:42. Al-Biqāʿī says no denier escaped God's reach, unlike a human pursuer, showing His knowledge and power: Pharaoh's army was drowned; Noah's deniers perished except those aboard the ark; Lot's towns were uprooted, overturned, stoned and flooded. Al-Bursawī similarly lists drowning Noah's people, overturning and stoning Lot's towns then burying them in foul water, and drowning Pharaoh's troops in the Red Sea or Nile; each met fitting recompense. Ibn ʿĀshūr adds that total destruction left none alive and compares 25:14."}, {"id": "69:10/q07/p2", "position": "The seizure is an unbearable, final punishment rather than a temporary warning.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī calls it indefensible and unbearable, and distinguishes it from punishment sent to warn and remind."}]}
{"id": "69:10/q08", "question": "How does the singular “taking” apply to those seized?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:10/q08/p1", "position": "It is one taking: Pharaoh and his people's drowning, or one taking distributed to each nation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives both according to whether the antecedent is Pharaoh's people alone or includes the other peoples, and compares 54:42."}]}
{"id": "69:10/q09", "question": "How is rābiya formed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:10/q09/p1", "position": "It is the active participle of rabā-yarbū, 'to increase,' with wāw changed to yāʾ after a kasra.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr gives the morphological derivation and sound change."}]}
{"id": "69:10/q10", "question": "What does rābiya say about the seizure?", "turns_on": "Whether increase describes intensity, comparison with other punishments, an extraordinary event, its destructive or lasting effect, or its continuation into the Hereafter.", "positions": [{"id": "69:10/q10/p1", "position": "It was severe, great, elevated, or increasing in severity.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās gloss it as severe in al-Ṭabarī; Mujāhid repeats in al-Māwardī, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr and al-Durr. Al-Mubarrad derives severity and greatness from increase; al-Naẓm calls it extreme in severity and explains rabā as increase and multiplication. Al-Majāz, al-Rāzī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bursawī, al-Ālūsī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī derive it from growth; Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares wealth, usury and 22:5, al-Qurṭubī and al-Bursawī compare the increment of usury. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the image of increase is borrowed for severity. Ibn Zayd says increase can be good or evil, citing guidance in 47:17 and punishment in 16:88. Al-Itqān calls 'severe' a Himyarī usage. Al-Elmalılı says the grip rises with disobedience."}, {"id": "69:10/q10/p2", "position": "It exceeded other peoples' or ordinary punishments.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says the seizure exceeded other afflictions; al-Wāḥidī reports it surpassed other peoples' punishment, and al-Zajjāj says it increased beyond events. Al-Jishumī says it surpassed every other blow while denying that it exceeded what was deserved. Al-Baghawī reports it surpassed earlier nations' punishments. Al-Kashshāf, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī connect greater severity to especially ugly deeds. Abū Ḥayyān's Mujāhid contrasts drowning and the overturning of towns. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this as an alternative to increased severity."}, {"id": "69:10/q10/p3", "position": "It was an extraordinary, overwhelming punishment outside the ordinary course.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba calls it high, overwhelming and much spoken of. Al-Jishumī calls it extraordinarily overwhelming; al-Ṭabrisī reports it as high, notorious and extraordinary. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports the extraordinary character as a separate alternative."}, {"id": "69:10/q10/p4", "position": "It was a destructive punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī gives this gloss, as transmitted by al-Māwardī and Ibn Kathīr."}, {"id": "69:10/q10/p5", "position": "It means remaining in God's punishment forever.", "reasons": "Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī gives this explanation in al-Māwardī."}, {"id": "69:10/q10/p6", "position": "The punishment grew from worldly destruction into punishment in the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says Pharaoh's worldly punishment continued into the afterlife and cites 71:25, drowning followed by fire. Study Quran applies the same sequence to Noah's people, with the Hereafter still more severe."}]}
{"id": "69:10/q11", "question": "What does this seizure teach about deserved punishment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:10/q11/p1", "position": "Punishment is earned by people's deeds, and rebellion against a divine envoy deserves a rebel's punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says the seizure proves deserved punishment against the Mujabbiṣa and says even a blow greater than others is not more than deserved. Iṣlāḥī likens the messenger to the universe's King's envoy."}]}
{"id": "69:10/q12", "question": "What role does the verse play in the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:10/q12/p1", "position": "It warns later deniers and awakens discerning readers through the earlier peoples' fate.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī names Quraysh as the warning's immediate audience and people of understanding as its wider audience."}, {"id": "69:10/q12/p2", "position": "It shifts the examples from pre-Islamic Arabian disbelievers to opponents of prophets in the Judeo-Christian tradition.", "reasons": "Study Quran describes this movement in the passage."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q01", "question": "What does the water's transgression mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ṭaghā describes physical excess, loss of the keepers' measured control, simple appearance, or an inward flood.", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q01/p1", "position": "The floodwater rose, grew abundant, and exceeded its customary bounds, covering the land.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās locates the abundance in the nights Noah's people drowned; Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and ʿAṭāʾ gloss it as rising or increasing. Al-Jishumī defines ṭughyān as crossing a limit. Ibn Kathīr says this occurred by God's permission. Al-Biqāʿī says people could neither control nor resist it and it exceeded ordinary causes. Al-Bayḍāwī relates this flood to the prior destroyed peoples; the Study Quran identifies Noah's Flood and Ark."}, {"id": "69:11/q01/p2", "position": "The water exceeded its angelic keepers' measure and control; the exception accompanied divine anger.", "reasons": "ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and transmitted prophetic reports say rain and wind ordinarily arrive by known measure, but Noah's water and ʿĀd's wind overwhelmed their keepers (69:6–7). Saʿīd describes the water's anger at God's anger. Al-Qurṭubī notes a raised version earlier in the sūra; al-Ālūsī says the Ṣaḥīḥayn and others corroborate ʿAlī's report. Al-Rāzī says the keepers could not tell how much escaped; Ibn Kathīr describes release beyond reservoirs. Al-Burṣawī offers this as an alternative level the angels could not contain."}, {"id": "69:11/q01/p3", "position": "The water appeared.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī transmits this gloss from Ibn Abī Najīḥ."}, {"id": "69:11/q01/p4", "position": "The overflowing water is the flood of prime matter.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī offers an inward reading."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q02", "question": "How high did the floodwater rise?", "turns_on": "The reports give different heights and different reference points.", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q02/p1", "position": "It rose fifteen cubits above everything, described also as fifteen above the highest mountain.", "reasons": "Qatāda is repeatedly named; al-Wāḥidī's broader report names Qatāda and Muqātil. Al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Burṣawī and al-Ālūsī specify the highest mountain rather than 'everything.'"}, {"id": "69:11/q02/p2", "position": "It rose forty cubits above everything.", "reasons": "Muqātil gives this measurement."}, {"id": "69:11/q02/p3", "position": "It rose more than fifteen cubits.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī cites Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid for this alternative."}, {"id": "69:11/q02/p4", "position": "It rose five hundred cubits above everything.", "reasons": "Al-Burṣawī cites this report."}, {"id": "69:11/q02/p5", "position": "It rose above the highest mountain, without a specified distance.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī say

{"id": "69:11/q03", "question": "Why is the floodwater described as transgressing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q03/p1", "position": "Its rising is pictured as overpowering arrogance or tyranny, intensifying the force of the flood.", "reasons": "Al-Rummānī says literal 'rose' becomes a scene of overpowering force. Al-Burhān locates the metaphor in arrogance and water, united by excessive elevation. Al-Itqān describes borrowing abstract arrogance for perceptible abundance. Ibn ʿĀshūr likens the unprecedented force to a tyrant overstepping against people."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q04", "question": "What caused Noah's flood in this account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q04/p1", "position": "God punished Noah's people for persistent unbelief, sin, and rejection of his message; Noah's supplication preceded the flood.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr mentions their worship of other gods and Noah's prayer. Al-Burṣawī and al-Ālūsī specify denial of revealed teaching on resurrection. Kur'an Yolu cites 7:59–64 and 11:25–49 for the rebellious people drowned and believers saved."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q05", "question": "What does 'We carried you' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q05/p1", "position": "It means putting people aboard a vessel and rescuing them through its movement.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī lists boarding and saving, citing Noah's vessel (54:13) and carrying on land and sea (17:70). Ibn ʿĀshūr extends the basic sense of placing one body on another to passengers in a moving vessel. Al-Burṣawī and al-Ālūsī stress raising them above floodwater until it receded, beyond mere boarding."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q06", "question": "Who is addressed as 'you' in the carrying?", "turns_on": "Whether the address is to the saved passengers themselves or to descendants by ancestral identification; al-Ālūsī disputes indwelling as its mechanism.", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q06/p1", "position": "Later descendants are addressed through their ancestors who were carried in Noah's ark, often described as present in their forefathers' loins.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Māwardī, al-Wāḥidī and others give the loins formulation. Al-Naḥḥās and Asad call the address figurative or metonymic; al-Jishumī compares ancestral praise and blame (2:91). Al-Māwardī cites al-ʿAbbās's poem tracing the Prophet through ancestral loins to Noah's ship and Nusr's drowning. Al-Wāḥidī and Study Quran compare 36:41. Al-Burṣawī says ancestral rescue made descendants' existence possible. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī invokes humanity as one kind and group. Al-Ālūsī also offers an omitted possessive, 'your ancestors'; al-Elmalılı adds preservation of the believing line. Al-Iṣlāḥī specifies Quraysh as Noah's descendants."}, {"id": "69:11/q06/p2", "position": "The 'you' are the original believers rescued aboard the ark, who became later generations' ancestors.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu says they came ashore after the water receded."}, {"id": "69:11/q06/p3", "position": "Descendants are addressed as their ancestors through indwelling.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports and rejects this explanation as remote."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q07", "question": "What inward meanings are given to being carried?", "turns_on": "The two reports locate the carrying in different spiritual processes.", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q07/p1", "position": "The Real flows upon spirits according to appointed divisions and reveals a mystery at spiritual stations.", "reasons": "Al-Qāsim argues bodies did not yet exist and spirits cannot literally bear a current."}, {"id": "69:11/q07/p2", "position": "God carried humanity by His signs and allotted its times by His measures.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī relates this to God's touching Adam's side and bringing out his descendants."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q08", "question": "What is al-jāriya?", "turns_on": "Whether the definite expression denotes Noah's singular ark, sailing ships generally, or an inward ark.", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q08/p1", "position": "It is Noah's sailing ark, a ship called jāriya because it moves over water.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Zayd, Mujāhid and al-Suddī gloss it as ship. Al-Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī also note jāriya for a young woman, explaining it by flowing youthful beauty. Al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī and Ibn ʿĀshūr cite 55:24; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn cite 42:32. Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī give the riddle of ninety 'maidens' inside one ship; al-Elmalılı cites the same poetic line and 11:42. Al-Biqāʿī sees an exceptional vessel sailing where water would normally drown. Al-Qurṭubī says Noah, his children and the ancestors of all earth's people were aboard."}, {"id": "69:11/q08/p2", "position": "It refers broadly to sailing ships as a divine favor to those addressed.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Mahdawī's broader reading."}, {"id": "69:11/q08/p3", "position": "The ark signifies religious law, comprising scientific and practical perfection.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī's inward reading."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q09", "question": "Why use the word al-jāriya for the ark?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q09/p1", "position": "The expression evokes the ship's motion and has become a conventional name for a vessel.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, al-Wāḥidī and al-Jishumī derive it from sailing on water. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn say usage is established. Ibn ʿĀshūr says an omitted safīna is described by its motion and the epithet nearly became a name; al-Biqāʿī says the quality substitutes for its noun. Al-Elmalılı says the definite singular points to Noah's ark and hints at descendants preserved in the current of ancestral loins."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q10", "question": "How does 'in the vessel' attach grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q10/p1", "position": "The preposition belongs to an omitted circumstantial phrase describing the people as safe aboard the moving ship.", "reasons": "Al-Burṣawī and al-Ālūsī say fī is not governed directly by ḥamalnā."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q11", "question": "Who truly carried and protected the passengers?", "turns_on": "Whether direct divine protection or God's command through Noah explains the attribution.", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q11/p1", "position": "God alone protected and saved them; the ark was an outward means.", "reasons": "Al-Burṣawī says rescue depended solely on divine protection. Al-Ālūsī calls the ship an outward means. Al-Elmalılı says its use displayed divine power and faith was the spiritual reason for boarding."}, {"id": "69:11/q11/p2", "position": "The carrying is attributed to God because He instructed Noah to build the ark and put the passengers aboard.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the attribution a grammatical metaphor and cites 23:27."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q12", "question": "What is reported about the ark's form?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different physical features.", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q12/p1", "position": "It was 1,300 cubits long and 600 wide, and sailed between waters.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī transmits this from al-Ḥasan."}, {"id": "69:11/q12/p2", "position": "It was shaped like a bird's breast so travel in water resembled motion through air.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says God gave Noah this instruction."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q13", "question": "Who first built a ship?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q13/p1", "position": "Noah was the first, building it by God's revelation and protection.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī makes this claim."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q14", "question": "What happened to life outside the ark?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q14/p1", "position": "The flood engulfed the earth; all humans and nonhumans outside the ark drowned, while its believers survived.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says none outside survived. Ibn Kathīr says humanity descends from Noah; Kur'an Yolu says the believers survived and cites 7:59–64 and 11:25–49."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q15", "question": "What lesson does the rescue give later people?", "turns_on": "Whether the stress falls on gratitude for rescue or warning from the drowned.", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q15/p1", "position": "It calls descendants to gratitude for their ancestors' rescue and their own continued existence.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says God favors them as descendants of the saved; Ibn ʿĀshūr extends the gratitude to all people descended from the rescued group. Al-Iṣlāḥī says Quraysh indirectly received the favor through believing ancestors."}, {"id": "69:11/q15/p2", "position": "It warns the present community to obey its messenger, or it may suffer punishment like Noah's deniers.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī relates the destroyed peoples' stories to this warning; al-Iṣlāḥī applies it to Quraysh. Al-Suddī says an attentive ear preserves the story of Noah's people punished for disobedience."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q16", "question": "How does Noah's episode fit the preceding sequence?", "turns_on": "The sources explain either the account's link to 'those before him' or its placement at the end.", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q16/p1", "position": "It completes the destroyed peoples' examples by showing all opponents destroyed and those agreeing with messengers saved.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says this answers the question raised by 'those before him' (69:9–10). Al-Bayḍāwī says the flood supports the preceding account."}, {"id": "69:11/q16/p2", "position": "Noah's people come last though historically first; their earthwide story closes the sequence and recalls the messengers' history.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says Thamūd comes first as the closest destroyed people to Mecca and thus the stronger nearby warning, while Noah's people were known to all later people. Al-Iṣlāḥī says the brief closing mention evokes prophetic history."}]}

{"id": "69:11/q18", "question": "What role does poetry study have in interpretation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q18/p1", "position": "It gives access to linguistic wisdom and breadth needed by interpreters.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī challenges opponents of poetry study to test their mastery of the disciplines they already accept as necessary."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q19", "question": "What is said about the Quran's challenge and eloquence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q19/p1", "position": "The Quran's unmatched speech proved Muhammad's message through the Arabs' highest art.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says listeners could identify poets' styles, yet eloquent Arabs facing the challenge of 2:23 recognized the Quran as neither poetry, soothsaying nor madness; al-Walīd is an example. The miracle suited the age's eloquence, as Moses' suited magic and Jesus' medicine."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q20", "question": "What senses of qatl are recorded in the ancillary lexical discussion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q20/p1", "position": "The root spans killing, enemies, figurative thorough knowledge or mixing, and expressions of amorous yielding or a heart struck by love.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī distinguishes qatl, qitāl and maqātil; cites a poem using aqtāl for enemies and Imruʾ al-Qays for a heart felled by love; explains 'killing' wine with water as mixing it."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q21", "question": "What does the ancillary discussion say about derivation and the word kalima?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q21/p1", "position": "Greater derivation tests root-letter permutations; kalima can also name extended linked speech by part-for-whole metaphor.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says triliteral roots have six permutations, though few use all, and larger roots are harder. He groups five k-l-m permutations around force or intensity, with examples of speech striking mind, wound, rough ground, completion, punch, low-water well, and firming dough or power. He says a poem, testimony, or good utterance can be called one word because connected speech forms a unity."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q22", "question": "What accounts of divine oaths appear in the ancillary discussion?", "turns_on": "The ancillary authorities classify divine oaths by object, purpose, and expression.", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q22/p1", "position": "An oath by created things implies their Creator, while God may swear by what He wills and people only by God.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī al-Iṣbaʿ argues an effect presupposes an agent; al-Ḥasan states the distinction between divine and human oaths."}, {"id": "69:11/q22/p2", "position": "God's oath by the Prophet's life marks his exceptional rank.", "reasons": "The scholars and Ibn ʿAbbās cite 15:72; Ibn ʿAbbās says no other person's life was sworn by."}, {"id": "69:11/q22/p3", "position": "Divine oaths can emphasize excellence or benefit, take different objects, and appear explicitly or implicitly.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī gives Sinai and the secure city for excellence and fig and olive for benefit (95:1–3). Another classification lists God's essence, acts and creation (91:5–7; 53:1; 52:1–2). Al-Itqān notes implicit oaths signaled by lām or inferred (3:186; 19:71); Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī distinguishes ambiguous report/oath forms from forms taking an oath response (57:8; 2:63; 58:18; 3:187; 24:53)."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q23", "question": "How are Quranic verse endings described in the ancillary discussion?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q23/p1", "position": "Their patterned sounds serve meaning and mark pauses while adding rhythmic beauty.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports al-Rummānī's distinction between identical and neighboring final letters, with examples at 20:2, 52:2, 1:3 and 50:1. Al-Rummānī says meaning governs sound. Abū Hilāl al-ʿAskarī says Quranic patterned prose surpasses human sajʿ in meaning, clarity and elegance; most rhetoricians resisted a sharp separation, with 100:1 cited."}]}
{"id": "69:11/q24", "question": "How does the flood's time function in the sentence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:11/q24/p1", "position": "The familiar time of Noah's flood supplies the temporal condition for God's carrying the people in the vessel.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr treats the well-known flood as the time indicated by lammā."}]}
{"id": "69:12/q01", "question": "What does “it” in “make it a reminder” refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun points to the physical vessel, the preceding rescue and drowning, the carrying, the broader account, or the sūra’s future Judgment; al-Rāzī tests whether the following pronoun can share its antecedent.", "positions": [{"id": "69:12/q01/p1", "position": "The flood event: the drowning of Noah’s deniers and rescue of the believers.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and al-Wāḥidī name both sides of the event. Al-Rāzī prefers it because both feminine pronouns should have the same antecedent and an ear cannot retain the Ark itself. Al-Ālūsī also prefers it. {"id": "69:25/q11", "question": "Why does he wish he had not received his book?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish anguish at disclosure and reckoning, a desire to escape punishment itself, a wish for death or nonresurrection, and a possible hopeful utterance.", "positions": [{"id": "69:25/q11/p1", "position": "The record exposes ugly deeds, his reckoning and painful fate, causing shame, grief and regret.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Qurtubi add a wish not to know the reckoning; Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Nasafi, Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi and others emphasize shameful deeds. Qashani says he wishes for death; Kuranyolu says he wishes death had ended everything."}, {"id": "69:25/q11/p4", "position": "He may voice the wish in hope.", "reasons": "Mawardi gives this as one possibility, alongside the account that he was concealed and has now been exposed."}]}

{"id": "69:25/q13", "question": "What form of ليتني is also used by Arabs?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:25/q13/p1", "position": "Some Arabs drop its nūn, as they do after إن.", "reasons": "Nahhas cites Arab usage of this omission."}]}
{"id": "69:25/q14", "question": "What does the passive لَمْ أُوتَ express?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:25/q14/p1", "position": "It expresses his wish that he had not been given the record.", "reasons": "Bursevi explicitly explains the passive form in this negative clause as not being given the book."}]}
{"id": "69:25/q15", "question": "What is the final hāʾ in كِتَٰبِيَهْ, and may it remain when speech continues?", "turns_on": "Whether the pausal grammatical rule can count against an established connected recitation; Abu Hayyan appeals to mass transmission, while Nahhas appeals to grammar and pausing at the rasm.", "positions": [{"id": "69:25/q15/p1", "position": "It is hāʾ al-sakt, a still pausal letter that clarifies the preceding vowel.", "reasons": "Nahhas says it clarifies the vowel at pause. {"id": "69:25/q16", "question": "How is the final hāʾ of كِتَٰبِيَهْ and related forms read?", "turns_on": "The readers differ about connected pronunciation and which words take omission; all reports here retain the hāʾ at pause where specified, and Jishumi gives conflicting attributions for related forms.", "positions": [{"id": "69:25/q16/p1", "position": "Most readers retain the hāʾ in both connected speech and pause.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan includes book, reckoning, wealth, power and mā hiyah at 101:10. {"id": "69:25/q17", "question": "How does this left-hand passage relate to the right-hand passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "69:25/q17/p1", "position": "It counterposes the accepted right-hand recipient to warn through the rejected person's fate.", "reasons": "Biqai says the accepted person comes first to encourage hope, then the rejected person warns against his deeds. Wahidi calls al-Aswad the brother of the person associated with 69:19; Elmalili contrasts a friendly favorable review with a hostile adverse one."}]}
